doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Why the big bands declined
summary: His theories: cost, bebop, the recording strike and singers like Sinatra.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Well after World War II, what happened to swing in your estimation? The big band era?

Well there are so many theories about this, the demise of the big band and everything. I think largely economic, it cost some money. And then the beboppers came along with a smaller group, and probably lower overhead, and they played such interesting things that you can’t fault it you know, but I think that that did contribute to the demise of the big band, I don’t know. There are many theories, everybody’s got their own.
Because — that the audience didn’t understand what the bop players were doing so much, or they couldn’t dance to it. That’s part of it I guess.

I think so. Well yeah, that is one of the theories that killed the bands in that respect. I don’t know. Another thing, excuse me, another thing that was a contributing factor was the recording strike and the singers. I mean singers became the thing. Oh — I love Frank Sinatra, but I mean he didn’t help the big bands. In a way he helped, but in a way he killed the big bands, because singers became so popular and they didn’t need a band except to go in the studio and record or something, or do a show.
It didn’t necessarily depend on who was backing them up. It was just a nameless orchestra.
Right if you had a good arrangement with a good conductor and you go and record, or you go and do a concert at Carnegie Hall or something, they didn’t have a road band.
